near_miss.why_not: Russian grief gesture is not Homeric collapse striking the ground with the forehead; the other supplied Greek passages also lack this collocation.

A Norse prohibited-kin killing list, an Atharvan divine genealogy, and a Russian slander complaint use cognate kin terms but different relations and speech acts; no distinctive inherited enumeration established.

Repeated Russian drink epithet contrasts with Latvian genitive honey plus abstract sweetness in a marriage/bitter-hops contrast. Cognate vocabulary and a predictable taste association do not establish inheritance of the same figure. Searches found Vedic sweet honey/drink and Homeric sweet wine, recorded separately as a lead; Slavic slad- is not simply cognate with Vedic svād-/Greek hēd-.
Slab partner describes Agni with ghee, not tears; hot-tears parallel found outside slab and recorded as search lead.
Atharvan partner has nocturnal flying demons but neither the paired duration nor the numeral. Ordinary night vocabulary is insufficient.
Russian smoke issuing from a fabulous horse and Latin volcanic smoke share a physical image but no sufficiently distinctive shared phrasing beyond smoke and motion.
Serbian apostrophe compares night with a heart full of sorrow. Norse impersonal descriptions of nightfall lack fullness and the heart comparison. Cognate night and darkness alone are predictable.

Russian winds are violent; Sanskrit epic has a fragrant auspicious breeze. Shared verb with a renewed wind noun is ordinary weather language; wider Atharvan cognate noun-verb figures are a search lead, not proof for the slab pair.
Russian palace/cosmos parallelism or birth setting differs from Latvian star falling into sea. Locating stars in the sky is not distinctive enough.
Russian horse traverses hills, Latin hills return echoes. Repeated hill nouns reflect different syntax and figures; no inherited formula established.
Russian warm-spring epithet and Latin spring bringing warmth describe an ordinary seasonal property with different syntax; no distinctive traditional collocation shown.

near_miss.lead: Wolves and foxes; feeding corpses to wolves
near_miss.why_not: Herodotus discusses animal size and burial, not slain enemies feeding scavengers. Wider searches found Russian feeding formula but no adequate cross-branch feeding-wolves witness in the inspected hits; Norse hits include wolf names and other unrelated contexts.

near_miss.lead: Lie down and sleep at night
near_miss.why_not: Cognate sleep vocabulary and some lying-down verbs occur in routine narration. Russian maritime dream/marriage contexts differ from Norse night lodging; Latin sleep covering eyes is a different figure.

near_miss.lead: Husband’s kin in a woman’s lament
near_miss.why_not: The Greek context includes cognate brothers-in-law, sisters-in-law and both parents-in-law, a notable social parallel. But Russian enumerates household members with numerals; Helen contrasts potentially hostile relatives with a consistently kind father-in-law. No stable order, distinctive shared predicate or larger inherited wording. Corpus search confirms ordinary in-law pairs in Serbian and translated OHG; these do not resolve inheritance versus predictable kin enumeration.

Russian horse makes springs; Atharvan goat has purified hooves, and another charm compares speech from below to a frog in a cow hoofprint. Neither supplied partner continues the spring-creation wording.

near_miss.why_not: Mother-earth occurs in Russian context, not the supplied Norse anatomy description or Armenian geographical measurements. External Atharvan parallel recorded separately.

near_miss.lead: Wolf and heart in a charm
near_miss.why_not: Russian assigns steel to the heart and wolf qualities to legs; Atharvan text has the wolf’s heart. The cognate heart and wolf are not linked by the same syntactic relation. Both being charms cannot repair that mismatch.
Russian blood after a serpent encounter has no matching serpent-action predicate in the short Welsh hostage/blood line. Blood vocabulary alone does not support an inherited serpent-slaying phrase.

search_lead.cognate: Russian Горячи and Greek θερμά continue the warm/hot root *gʷher-; слезы and δάκρυα are not here treated as cognates.
search_lead.argument: Hot is an agreeing epithet of tears in both traditions, in emotional distress and adjacent to speech. Russian preceding context describes tears rolling. Possible inherited epithet with renewal of the tear noun; physiological obviousness and late Russian attestation limit the argument. Supplied Agni partner is unsuitable.

search_lead.cognate: Russian матушку (diminutive of мать) and Vedic mātā continue *méh₂tēr; Russian землю and Vedic pṛthivī are different earth words.
search_lead.argument: Russian context before the anchor identifies earth as mother; Atharvan apposition likewise makes earth mother, paired with father sky. This is a possible inherited personification with lexical renewal, not an equation of the entire Russian moist-earth formula. Russian giant-strength narrative differs from ritual genealogy. Neither slab partner supplies it.

search_lead.cognate: Russian меду, Greek μέθυ and Vedic madhu- continue *médʰu. Greek ἡδύ and Vedic svādu- agree etymologically; Russian сладкий is a different formation, not that exact cognate adjective.
search_lead.argument: Sweetness qualifies a drink in banquet/ritual settings. Greek wine versus Russian mead illustrates semantic divergence of the drink word; the Russian adjective would require renewal. A wider comparison is worth review, but sweet drink is an obvious combination and cannot alone prove inheritance. Latvian slab partner nominalizes sweetness in a marriage metaphor.

search_lead.cognate: Russian Повфютъ (read повеют) and вфтры (read ветры), and Vedic vā- and vāta-, all continue *h₂weh₁- with different noun suffixes.
search_lead.argument: A cognate subject-verb figure winds blow is preserved more exactly by Atharvan wording than by the slab epic partner with pavana. Russian OCR obscures the forms. Wind action is semantically predictable and ritual rain context differs from Russian narrative, so this remains only a search lead.

error.correct_reading: Sveinn, nominative personal name, the king speaking.
error.evidence: The following context calls him king; the preceding speech names his kinsman Knútr. This is not common noun sveinn or reflexive swé.

error.correct_reading: Past participle of reyna, to test/experience.
error.evidence: With fær and the preceding strength description, the sense is that he can scarcely test his own strength; not reinn and not a sift/separate cognate.

error.correct_reading: Повѣютъ / normalized повеют, third-person plural future of повеять.
error.evidence: Plural winds are the subject; OCR ф stands for ѣ, as also in the adjacent wind noun.

error.correct_reading: вѣтры / normalized ветры, nominative plural of ветер.
error.evidence: Subject of повеют; the same noun is repeated in preceding context.

error.correct_reading: крѣпкаго / normalized крепкого, genitive singular adjective agreeing with булату.
error.evidence: The protective charm assigns the heart strong steel; the dollar sign and и obscure the adjective, not a separate lexeme.
